Nociceptor

Noradrenaline reaches the nociceptor in two places. At its central terminals, noradrenaline from descending brainstem fibres acts on α2A adrenoceptors, which through Gi reduce the release of transmitters onto dorsal horn neurons. At its endings in the joint, noradrenaline and adrenaline from sympathetic fibres and the blood act on β2 adrenoceptors, which through Gs sensitise the endings and after stress switch to Gi. Receptors let the noradrenaline go when their G protein is activated, and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inactivates it by methylation to normetanephrine. People with low COMT activity are more sensitive to pain, a COMT variant is linked to OA pain, and in rats COMT inhibition raises pain through β2 and β3 adrenoceptors.

Spinal nociceptive neuron

Noradrenaline released by descending pathways in the spinal dorsal horn acts on α2A adrenoceptors, which couple to Gi and dampen pain, and on β2 adrenoceptors, which couple to Gs and Gi. Receptors let the noradrenaline go when their G protein is activated, and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inactivates it by methylation to normetanephrine. Lower COMT activity raises pain sensitivity, and in rats COMT inhibition raises pain through β2 and β3 adrenoceptors.

Colour

Red raises pain, blue relieves it, and olive is shared signalling whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. α2A signalling is blue, β2 signalling red, COMT blue. Noradrenaline is olive, as it feeds both.
